summary: Matthew and Luke trace Jesus’ family line: Matthew from Abraham through David’s royal sons to Joseph, Luke from Joseph back through David to Adam and God.
key_insight: Matthew repeats “begot” thirty-nine times, then breaks his own pattern. He does not say Joseph begot Jesus; he calls Joseph “the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus.” Luke does the same with “as was supposed.” Both family trees guard the virgin birth.
story: Matthew opens his Gospel with a title: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the Son of David, the Son of Abraham.” He begins with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, then Judah and his brothers. {Mt}

The line passes through Perez, Judah’s son by Tamar; through Boaz, born to Salmon by Rahab; and through Obed, born to Boaz by Ruth. Then “Jesse begot David the king,” and David fathered Solomon by “her who had been the wife of Uriah.” {Mt}

From Solomon the list follows the kings of Judah, good and bad, down to Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the exile to Babylon. After the exile come Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, and then a line of names down to Jacob, who “begot Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus who is called Christ.” Matthew counts fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the exile, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ. {Mt}

Luke places his list later, when Jesus began His ministry “at about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph.” Instead of moving forward from Abraham, Luke climbs backward. Joseph was “the son of Heli,” and the line rises through Zerubbabel and Shealtiel to Nathan, “the son of David.” {Lk}

From David, Luke goes on through Jesse, Boaz and Judah to Abraham, and he does not stop there. He continues through Shem and Noah, Methuselah and Enoch, Seth and Adam, and ends: “the son of Adam, the son of God.” {Lk}
differences: Matthew moves forward from Abraham with “begot”; Luke moves backward from Jesus with “the son of” and goes all the way to Adam and God.
Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy; Luke places it after Jesus’ baptism, as His ministry begins.
Between David and Joseph the lists follow different sons of David: Matthew goes through Solomon and the kings, Luke through Nathan. Matthew names Joseph’s father as Jacob; Luke names Heli.
Matthew names four women besides Mary (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah) and arranges his list in three sets of fourteen. Luke names no women.
Both lists include Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, but Matthew calls Shealtiel the son of Jeconiah and Luke calls him the son of Neri.

fit.question: Matthew and Luke give different names for most of Jesus’ ancestors between David and Joseph. Matthew says Joseph’s father was Jacob; Luke says Heli. How can both be right?

points.label: Mary’s line in Luke
points.text: Many hold that Luke gives Mary’s ancestry. Luke tells the birth from Mary’s side, and his wording “(as was supposed) the son of Joseph” sets Joseph apart. Heli would then be Mary’s father, with Joseph counted as his son by marriage, while Matthew gives Joseph’s legal line through Solomon and the kings.

points.label: Two lines of Joseph
points.text: Others hold that both lists are Joseph’s: one his natural descent, the other his legal line as heir. Julius Africanus, writing around AD 220, passed on a tradition he said came from Jesus’ own relatives: Jacob and Heli were half brothers, and when one died childless the other married his widow to raise up a son in his brother’s name, in the manner of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). Joseph could then be counted as the son of both.

points.label: Shared names
points.text: Shealtiel and Zerubbabel appear in both lists. They may be the same two men, with the lines crossing through a legal heir, or different men with common names.

fit.note: Faithful scholars hold different explanations, but each fits the ways ancient families traced legal and natural descent, and none requires an error.
fit.short: Many think Luke gives Mary’s line and Matthew Joseph’s; others see both as Joseph’s, one natural and one legal. Views differ.

scene.label: Why family lines mattered
scene.text: Israel kept careful family records. After the exile, men who could not prove their descent were kept out of the priesthood (Ezra 2:62). The Messiah was expected to come from David’s family (2 Samuel 7:12–16), so a public line from David was part of Jesus’ claim.

scene.label: Four surprising women
scene.text: Ancient family lists usually named only men. Matthew names Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba. Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and Ruth a Moabite. Tamar’s and Bathsheba’s stories involve deep family sin (Genesis 38; 2 Samuel 11), and Matthew calls Bathsheba only “the wife of Uriah,” a Hittite.

scene.label: Three fourteens
scene.text: Matthew shapes Israel’s history into three periods: the patriarchs to David, the kings to the exile, the exile to the Christ. To do it he leaves out some names, such as three kings between Joram and Uzziah (1 Chronicles 3:11–12). Jewish lists often skipped generations, and “begot” could mean was the ancestor of. Some note that the Hebrew letters of David’s name add up to fourteen.

scene.label: Zerubbabel
scene.text: God had said that even if Jeconiah were a signet on His right hand, He would pluck him off (Jeremiah 22:24). Yet to Zerubbabel, Jeconiah’s grandson in Matthew’s list, God promised, “I will take you” and “make you like a signet ring” (Haggai 2:23). Zerubbabel led the people home and rebuilt the temple. David’s line was cut down but not cut off, and both lists pass through him.

witnesses.matthew: Opens his whole Gospel with the genealogy and its title: Jesus is the Son of David, the promised King, and the Son of Abraham, through whom all nations would be blessed. His three fourteens tell Israel’s story from promise to kingdom to exile and at last to the Christ, and his four women show grace reaching outsiders and sinners from the very first page.
witnesses.luke: Places the genealogy between the Father’s voice at the baptism, “You are My beloved Son” (Luke 3:22), and the devil’s challenge, “If You are the Son of God” (Luke 4:3). His list runs past Abraham to Adam, “the son of God,” presenting Jesus as the Savior of the whole human race, not of Israel alone.

seeing.reveals: Jesus has a real family history. He is the heir of David and the promised seed of Abraham, and He is also a true son of Adam, sharing the humanity of the whole race He came to save.
seeing.living: Matthew does not hide the scandals in Jesus’ family: Judah and Tamar, David and Uriah’s wife, kings who led Judah into idolatry. God kept His promise through people like these. Your family’s failures cannot cancel God’s promises, and your own past does not keep you out of the family Jesus is gathering.
seeing.ponder: Which part of your own story do you think is too broken for God to write into His purposes?

preaching.big_idea: Through failure and exile, God kept His promise to Abraham and David, and it led to Jesus.
outline: The promise named: Son of David, Son of Abraham (1)
Kings who failed and an exile that seemed final (7–11)
A hope kept alive to the Christ (12–17)
preaching.watch_for: Matthew’s first words echo Genesis 5:1, “This is the book of the genealogy of Adam.” Matthew opens the New Testament the way Genesis opened the human story: with a new beginning in one Man.

title: The Family Line of Jesus
